title: Mud Kitchen
strapline: Real pans, real weather, invented recipes — the outdoor kitchen where mud is the main ingredient.
intent: Sustain rich pretend cooking play — cafés, birthday teas, potion shops — with roles, customers and menus that children run themselves.
Invent and follow recipes: three scoops of mud, a splash of water, a sprinkle of petals — sequencing, measuring and quantity in the most memorable form.
Investigate mixture and change: how water turns dry soil to paste, then slop; how a mud pie left in the sun goes hard and cracks.
Work with real tools and real risk, well managed — metal pans, wooden spoons, whisks, a proper handwashing routine after — building competence and trust.
Notice weather and seasons as working conditions: rain makes the best mud, frost makes the pans sparkle, summer bakes the pies.
Meet the small life in the soil — worms, woodlice, beetles — and learn to handle it gently or leave it be.
implementation: Stock it like a real kitchen: donated metal pans, ladles, whisks, sieves, muffin tins — real tools signal real respect for the play, and children rise to them.
Take a role and stay in it — be the fussy customer who orders 'worm soup with extra sprinkles', then let children run the kitchen.
Feed in kitchen language at the point of stirring: simmer, dollop, drizzle, sprinkle, thick, runny, gloopy.
Scribe or photograph children's invented recipes and pin them up laminated — the kitchen grows its own cookbook.
Frame the mess as a managed risk, not a problem: waterproofs on, sleeves up, a firm 'mud stays out of mouths', and an unhurried handwashing routine that children own.
Go out in the rain on purpose sometimes — puddle water and fresh mud transform the cooking, and children learn the weather is an ingredient.
When a worm turns up in the pie dish, pause the cooking: gentle hands, a good look, and back to the soil it goes.
key_questions: What's cooking today — can I see the menu?
How many scoops does your recipe need?
What happened to yesterday's pie we left on the shelf?
How could you make your mixture thicker?
What do you think the rain will do to the kitchen?
What should we do with this worm we've found?

impact.text: Children role play familiar cooking and café scenes — serving, ordering, feeding the baby — with props and friends around them.
Older children sustain a shared kitchen storyline, assigning roles — chef, waiter, customer — and negotiating who stirs and who serves.
Children narrate and direct their cooking — 'first the mud, now the leaves, don't touch it, it's hot' — running the play through talk.
Children scoop, pour, stir and whisk with one-handed tools, and use them with real intent — tapping the spoon, levelling the tin.
Children count scoops and spoonfuls into their recipes accurately, checking they have enough 'cakes' for every customer.
Children discover how mixing changes materials — dry soil to paste to slop — and that sun-baked pies go hard and crack.
Children connect weather to their play — hunting puddle water after rain, predicting frost will freeze the pans overnight.
Children treat the worms and woodlice they unearth gently, returning them to the soil without being asked.

enhancements: Herb pots within picking reach — rosemary, mint, lavender — so every recipe has a scent and a garnish.
A chalkboard menu and price list, plus a basket of leaf 'money' for the café till.
Muffin tins and petals, seed heads and gravel for transient-art 'cupcakes' photographed before the rain takes them.
Laminated recipe cards drawn from the children's own inventions — three scoops, two petals, one stir.
Balance scales and different-sized scoops to bring weight and measure into the mixing.
A 'pie shelf' for leaving creations out over days — the slow experiment of drying, cracking and washing away.
A bug viewer and soft brush stationed by the digging patch for whoever the digging uncovers.

playing_exploring: Children replay home and café life in mud, stretching what they know into invented dishes and potions.
The kitchen rewards bold having-a-go — plunging in, mixing, tasting the idea (never the mud).
active_learning: Getting a mixture 'just right' — thicker, runnier, more sprinkles — is trial, error and adjustment children choose to repeat.
Long cooking storylines hold concentration across a whole session, sometimes across days.
creating_thinking: Children invent recipes, menus and potion rules of their own, and change them when a better idea arrives.
They make links between weather, water and mud — and plan tomorrow's cooking around them.
